title: A Tiny Lip Point in 'Forgotten Island' Speaks Volumes
summary:
In DreamWorks' latest animated film, 'Forgotten Island', one tiny moment has caught fire online: the lip point. At a goodbye party for Raissa Molina, who is heading to Caltech, her best friend Jo arrives late and asks where Raissa is. An older woman points with her lips. It is a small visual gag, but audiences familiar with Filipino culture spotted it at once — and so did many Latino fans and others who use the same gesture.

The moment had been in the script since the first draft, director Joel Crawford told IndieWire, because the filmmakers wanted to draw on their own experience of Filipino culture. 'Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me,' Crawford said. Adding that detail felt like a celebration, he said, but it also made the characters feel real — and by being specific about the culture, it ended up being the most universal part of the movie, because it invites everyone in.

The lip point returns later in the film, when Jo does it herself — an animator suggested bringing it back after learning about its place in the culture. The film also has an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant, and the animation team found their own ways to honour Filipino culture. Jo's hand expressions were based on Filipino skater Margie Didal, while the villainous Manananggal's movements drew on choreography by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag.

Most of the story takes place on the island of Nakali, home to mythical creatures, and the visuals draw on 1990s Filipino art and anime from the same period. The directors also pushed the animation styles to show how people recall memories in different ways. That small, specific detail became a symbol of how the film approaches representation.
why_it_matters: Small details in films can make audiences from a culture feel seen, so the lip point shows how getting one detail right can speak to people far beyond that culture.

background_read: Filipino culture comes from the Philippines, a country in Southeast Asia with its own languages, food, art and stories.
In everyday life there, people sometimes point with their lips instead of a finger, a small gesture that many people grow up using without thinking about it.
Animated films are made by artists who draw and move characters frame by frame, and small details like gestures can make those characters feel like real people.
When filmmakers include details from a real culture, audiences who share that culture can feel seen, and other viewers can learn something new.
